prize_parts.citation: for the invention of the optical lattice clock based on magic-wavelength trapping and its realisation at the 10^-18 level of fractional uncertainty

statement.case_for: I keep optical lattice clocks as my single-part preference and I do not change my configuration from round 1. Having read the full exchange, the case has strengthened in the one respect that matters to me as a former chair: the committee is asked to identify the topic and the people responsible for the original work, and for B015 every file, including those of members who ranked it low, agrees on the attribution. Katori supplied the originating idea, trapping many neutral atoms at a magic wavelength so that the light shift cancels while Lamb-Dicke confinement and many-atom averaging are retained, and built the first strontium lattice clock. Ye took the same architecture to the systematic-uncertainty frontier near 10^-18. The result is quantitative, has been reproduced across species (Sr, Yb) and institutions, and the inter-laboratory comparisons test the uncertainty budgets and do not merely repeat one design. As an experimentalist who works on quantitative measurement, I give weight to that kind of independent confirmation. I also weighed whether a topological prize or a two-part package would be a better use of this year, and I conclude that it would not, for the reasons given below.
statement.case_against: The real weakness is novelty relative to the 2005 prize (Hall, Haensch) and the 2012 prize (Wineland, Haroche), and Eriksson is right that the committee must say why the lattice clock is a separate invention, not assert it. My answer is that the comb is a ruler for optical frequencies and the single ion is a control achievement, whereas the lattice clock resolves a different conflict, long interrogation of thousands of atoms against trap-induced light shifts, and no earlier citation describes it. That answer holds only if the citation is worded around the magic-wavelength lattice and its realisation and not around optical clocks in general. The second weakness is that a two-name credit leaves out other leading contributors (Lemonde, Lisdat, Ludlow, Lemke, Bloom, Hinkley and the ion-clock groups). I accept that this is a genuine simplification, but no member has proposed a different or additional name, and the roles of Katori (concept, first clock) and Ye (accuracy frontier) are separable. Finally, a metrology prize can look less like a discovery of nature than neutrino astronomy or a new class of matter, and my own first-ranked field, topological insulators, is stronger on conceptual reach.

responses.point: Eriksson ranked B015 sixth because the 2005 frequency-comb prize covers part of Ye's route and because he judges its conceptual reach lower than a new class of matter, but he accepts it is the cleanest attribution and would support it over B039 or B009. He also argued that the topological case should be drafted around the effect and the materials and that the Mele and Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang omissions must be debated explicitly.
responses.response: On the overlap with 2005 I think the answer is in the wording, and I would propose the citation cover the magic-wavelength lattice clock and its realisation at 10^-18, with no mention of combs, spectroscopy or timekeeping in general. Ye's comb-based work is then context, not the credited achievement. On B018 I agree with you that omitting Mele is not a footnote, and your point that the HgTe experiment tested a specific prediction, so a citation naming only the experiment would misdescribe how the discovery happened, is the one that moved me most. I had put B018 first at opening, and your file persuades me that the committee cannot yet defend three names for it. I still regard it as the strongest condensed-matter alternative and would keep it first among my alternatives.

responses.point: Pearce, who moved from B014 to B015, asked that Kroll's Hall-laboratory connection be recorded formally and that the committee examine the comparison data directly to see whether Ye's 10^-18 budgets are independent of Katori's. He also keeps B014 as his first alternative and B003 as another.
responses.response: I agree that the committee should record Kroll's disclosure formally, since Ye is one of the two names, and I would weigh it as background and not as a disqualifying tie. It is documented as a doctoral-period research stay and not as a personal relationship. His preference is shared by five other members who have no such link, so removing it would not change the picture. On independence of the 10^-18 claim I agree with your request, and what I can add from the evidence in the files is that it rests on comparisons between different species and different laboratories linked by fibre and satellite, which tests each systematic budget separately. I cannot verify the numbers here, so I flag that as an item the committee should confirm from the published comparison data before the vote. On B003 versus B018 I still disagree with bundling the quantum anomalous Hall effect into the same prize, because it is a separate experimental achievement, but that argument matters only if we move to a topological prize.

responses.point: Danielsson holds B014 first as a discovery of nature, would rest the citation on the diffuse flux alone and not on source identification, and says B015 should be preferred if the committee judges clean attribution to outweigh breadth of discovery. He also finds the collaboration-size problem easier to defend than a split among competing theorists.
responses.response: I think that is a fair and honest statement of where we differ, and I accept that placing a new window on nature ahead of a better instrument is a judgement and not a measurable criterion. I would answer your comparison of credit problems this way. For B014 the difficulty is that two names stand for a collaboration of hundreds with AMANDA and DUMAND antecedents, so any prize would be partly an arbitrary cut, and Eriksson names Kowalski, Klein and Waxman as outside the credit. For B015 the credit is a division of roles between an originating idea and a realisation, and the omitted groups confirmed the result and did not originate it. I would not oppose B014 in a later year with a citation anchored on the diffuse flux as you propose, but this year I do not think it should displace a candidate where both the credit and the independent confirmation are clearer.

responses.point: Lindroth treats B015 as the single-achievement baseline that any two-part package must justify itself against, and would anchor the citation on the clock concept and its accuracy, not on later many-body extensions or the redefinition of the second.
responses.response: I accept that framing and it answers the chair's question about a two-part configuration for me. A second part with B030 or B014 would force one of Katori, Ye or a laureate of the second part out, since the limit is three people in total, and neither pairing improves the scientific case enough to justify dropping a credited name. B030 also has the maturity problem you raise, the mechanism of superconductivity is still debated and Cao is outside the credit. I therefore stay with a single part. I also agree with you and with Mehlig that the redefinition of the second should not appear in the citation, because that is a decision for the metrology bodies and the prize should stand on what has been demonstrated.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept that the lattice clock is a distinct invention from the 2005 and 2012 prizes, which depends on a citation worded around the magic-wavelength lattice and its realisation.
Whether two names can fairly represent a field with strong contributions from SYRTE, PTB, NIST and others, since no member has proposed a different third name.
Whether the 10^-18 comparisons between independent laboratories are as independent as the files suggest, which I cannot verify from the supplied material.
For the topological alternative, how the committee would handle Mele and Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, and whether Hasan (B018) or Xue (B003) is the better third name.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for B015, B018, B030 or the other shortlisted candidates, and I have no documented tie to Katori, Ye or any other credited name. I share an institution (Chalmers) with Goran Johansson, who has disclosed WACQT leadership relevant to B039, and I note that his preference for B015 carries no declared conflict. I agree that Kroll's disclosed research stay in the Hall laboratory, with which Ye is associated, should be recorded formally. My electron-microscopy work on oxide interfaces is not tied to any candidate, though I rated topological insulators first at opening and that field is a possible source of bias in my alternatives.
